newsitem.title: UK: Former British minister drops libel case.
newsitem.headline: Former British minister drops libel case.

text.p: A former Conservative minister on Monday dropped a libel action against a British newspaper and spared Prime Minister John Major the embarrassment of having to appear in court on the eve of his party's conference.

Former trade minister Neil Hamilton and political lobbyist Ian Greer dropped the action that was due to be heard in London's High Court on Tuesday. He denied newspaper allegations he accepted cash in exchange for asking parliamentary questions.
Guardian editor Alan Rusbridger said the two had agreed a "substantial contribution towards the Guardian's costs."
In a statement, Rusbridger said the decision not to proceed "must be one of the most astonishing legal cave-ins in the history of the law of libel".
Hamilton, maintaining his innocence, said in a statement that he was devastated at having to withdraw from the case which he said had personally cost him 150,000 pounds ($234,100).

"The reason why I am applying for leave to withdraw is not because I am anything other than totally innocent of the charges...but since a conflict of interest has now arisen between me and my co-plaintiffs," he said.

"The consequence of this is that the trial would have had to have been postponed to enable new sets of lawyers to go through the huge volume of papers and prepare the case afresh at enormously increased cost," he added. Major had been subpoenaed to give evidence along with deputy premier Michael Heseltine in what threatened to be an explosive case on the eve of the ruling Conservative party's annual conference.

Major hopes to use the Conservatives' week-long conference beginning October 8 to repair party rifts over Europe and put to rest lingering allegations of sleaze that have dogged his party since he won a five-year term in 1992.

Hamilton and Greer, who works for some of Britain's biggest businesses, were suing the left-leaning Guardian for a reported one million pounds ($1.5 million) for its "cash-for-questions" report in 1994.
That accused Hamilton of accepting money from Mohammed al-Fayed, the owner of London's luxury Harrods department store, in return for tabling questions in parliament.
Hamilton, who resigned his junior ministerial position over the allegations, claimed he was a victim of "foully-motivated rumour and a media witchhunt" and vowed to clear his name.
The Conservative Party has endured a string of "sleaze" resignations. Nearly 20 party members have quit following various allegations of impropriety since Major took office in November 1990.
The deteriorating situation propelled Major to appoint a commission to recommend ways of raising the standards of British public life.
